tagline: One sentence that contains all of physics!
question_text: If all scientific knowledge were destroyed and only one sentence could be passed to the next generation, which statement would contain the most information in the fewest words?
option_a: (A) Energy is always conserved in every process
option_b: (B) All things are made of atoms that move in perpetual motion
option_d: (D) Light always travels in straight lines
correct_answer: Correct Answer: (B) All things are made of atoms that move in perpetual motion
equations_json: ["\\text{All things are made of atoms}", "\\text{They attract when apart, repel when squeezed}"]
audio_script: Feynman once asked: if all of science were destroyed and only one sentence survived, what should it be? His answer was the atomic hypothesis. That all things are made of atoms. Little particles that move around in perpetual motion, attracting each other when they are a little distance apart, but repelling upon being squeezed into one another. In that one sentence, there is an enormous amount of information about the world, if just a little imagination and thinking are applied. Think about a drop of water. If we magnify it a billion times, we see a teeming crowd of particles. Each oxygen atom with two hydrogens attached. They jiggle and bounce, attract and repel. This is the heart of all physics. Is sawaal mein Feynman ka sabse sundar vichaar hai. Yaad rakhiye, atoms hamesha ghoomte rehte hain, rukte nahi.

tagline: The molecule that makes life possible!
question_text: A water molecule consists of one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms. The angle between the two hydrogen atoms is approximately 105 degrees. What keeps the water molecules together in liquid water?
option_b: (B) Electrical attraction between the atoms of different molecules
correct_answer: Correct Answer: (B) Electrical attraction between the atoms of different molecules
equations_json: ["\\text{H}_2\\text{O molecule}", "\\text{Bond angle} \\approx 105^\\circ", "\\text{Electrical attraction holds molecules together}"]
audio_script: A water molecule is one oxygen with two hydrogens. The angle between the hydrogens is about one hundred five degrees. The oxygen has a slight negative charge and the hydrogens have slight positive charges. This tiny imbalance is what makes water so special. In liquid water, the positive hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the negative oxygen of another molecule. This electrical attraction holds the molecules together. It is why water stays liquid at room temperature. It is why ice floats. It is why life as we know it is possible. Feynman reminds us that this is all just electricity. The same force that makes a balloon stick to your hair is what keeps water together. Is sawaal mein aapko electrical force ki beauty dikhegi. Paani ki har boond mein physics chhupi hai.

question_text: What is the fundamental difference between ice, liquid water, and steam?
option_a: (A) The size of the water molecules changes
option_b: (B) The number of hydrogen atoms per oxygen changes
option_c: (C) The arrangement and motion of water molecules changes
option_d: (D) The color of the substance changes
correct_answer: Correct Answer: (C) The arrangement and motion of water molecules changes
equations_json: ["\\text{Ice: ordered lattice, small vibration}", "\\text{Water: random positions, larger vibration}", "\\text{Steam: molecules far apart, free motion}"]
audio_script: In ice, the water molecules are locked into a definite pattern. They vibrate in place, but they do not move around. When we heat the ice, the vibrations increase. At a certain temperature, the molecules shake themselves free from their positions. The rigid structure breaks down. Now the molecules can move around, but they still attract each other. This is liquid water. Heat it more, and the molecules move faster and faster. Eventually, the attraction is not enough to hold them together. They fly apart. This is steam. The molecule itself has not changed. It is the same H two O. Only the arrangement and the motion have changed. Feynman says this is the difference between solids, liquids, and gases. Yaad rakhiye, jiggling motion hi temperature hai. Zyada jiggling, zyada temperature.

question_text: What causes the pressure exerted by a gas on the walls of its container?
option_a: (A) The chemical reaction between gas and wall
option_b: (B) The gravitational attraction of gas molecules
option_c: (C) The continuous bombardment of gas molecules on the walls
option_d: (D) The magnetic field of the gas molecules
correct_answer: Correct Answer: (C) The continuous bombardment of gas molecules on the walls
audio_script: Why does a gas exert pressure? Feynman says imagine a room full of tennis balls, all bouncing around in perpetual motion. When they hit the wall, they push it. Each collision delivers a tiny impulse. A billion collisions per second create a steady force. That is pressure. If we double the number of molecules, we double the collisions. Pressure doubles. If we increase the temperature, the molecules move faster. They hit harder and more often. Pressure increases. This is the kinetic theory of gases. The pressure of a gas is simply the result of countless molecular bombardments. Is sawaal mein Feynman ki simple soch dikhti hai. Pressure koi mysterious force nahi hai. Yeh sirf atoms ka dhamaka hai.

tagline: Squeeze it and it gets hot!
question_text: When a gas is compressed slowly, its temperature increases. What is the microscopic reason for this?
option_a: (A) The gas molecules react chemically with the piston
option_b: (B) The molecules gain speed when they bounce off the moving piston
option_c: (C) The gravitational potential energy of the molecules increases
option_d: (D) The number of molecules increases during compression
correct_answer: Correct Answer: (B) The molecules gain speed when they bounce off the moving piston
equations_json: ["\\text{Piston moves inward}", "\\text{Molecule hits moving piston and speeds up}", "\\text{Temperature increases}", "PV^\\gamma = \\text{constant}"]
audio_script: Feynman gives a beautiful explanation of why a gas heats up when compressed. Imagine a molecule bouncing off a piston. If the piston is standing still, the molecule bounces back with the same speed. But if the piston is moving inward, the molecule bounces back faster. It picks up speed from the collision. Just like a ping pong ball hit by a forward-moving paddle comes off faster. So all the molecules in the vessel pick up speed. The temperature of the gas increases. This is why, under slow compression, a gas heats up. And under slow expansion, it cools down. Yaad rakhiye, har collision mein molecule piston se energy leta hai. Isliye compression se gas garam hoti hai.

question_text: Why does water evaporate faster when the air above it is dry and windy?
option_a: (A) Wind increases the temperature of water
option_b: (B) Dry air absorbs water molecules chemically
option_c: (C) Fewer water molecules return to the liquid when the air is dry
option_d: (D) Wind increases the attraction between water molecules
correct_answer: Correct Answer: (C) Fewer water molecules return to the liquid when the air is dry
equations_json: ["\\text{Evaporation rate} \\propto e^{-W/kT}", "\\text{Condensation rate depends on vapor density}", "\\text{Net evaporation when vapor removed}"]
audio_script: At the surface of water, molecules are always jiggling. From time to time, one gets hit a little harder than usual and escapes into the air. This is evaporation. But some molecules in the air come back and get stuck again. This is condensation. When the air above is dry, there are fewer water molecules in the air. So fewer come back. The number leaving stays the same, because it depends only on the jiggling of the water. So the water evaporates faster. If we blow the moist air away, we replace it with dry air. More molecules leave than return. The water disappears. This is why a fan helps to evaporate water. Feynman says turn on the fan! Is sawaal mein evaporation ka simple physics hai. Yaad rakhiye, jiggling tez, evaporation tez.

question_text: What happens microscopically when salt (sodium chloride) dissolves in water?
option_a: (A) Salt molecules melt into liquid salt
option_b: (B) Sodium and chlorine ions break free and are surrounded by water molecules
option_d: (D) Salt molecules simply float in the water unchanged
correct_answer: Correct Answer: (B) Sodium and chlorine ions break free and are surrounded by water molecules
equations_json: ["\\text{NaCl crystal}", "\\text{Na}^+ \\text{ and } \\text{Cl}^- \\text{ ions}", "\\text{Water molecules attract ions}", "\\text{Ions float freely in solution}"]
audio_script: Salt is a crystal. It is made of sodium ions and chlorine ions arranged in a regular pattern. Each sodium atom has lost one electron and is positive. Each chlorine atom has gained one electron and is negative. When we put salt in water, the water molecules are attracted to the ions. The negative oxygen end of a water molecule surrounds the positive sodium ion. The positive hydrogen ends surround the negative chlorine ion. This attraction pulls the ions away from the crystal. The crystal breaks apart. The ions float freely in the water, each surrounded by a shell of water molecules. Feynman says this is a dynamic process. Ions are leaving and rejoining all the time. Equilibrium is when the rates are equal. Is sawaal mein ion ka chemistry aur physics ka mel hai. Yaad rakhiye, paani ke molecules dipoles hote hain.

question_text: What is the fundamental difference between a physical process and a chemical reaction?
option_b: (B) Chemical reactions rearrange the partners that atoms are attached to
option_c: (C) Physical processes change the number of atoms
option_d: (D) There is no difference at all
correct_answer: Correct Answer: (B) Chemical reactions rearrange the partners that atoms are attached to
audio_script: Feynman says: what happens when carbon burns in oxygen? An oxygen molecule comes near the carbon. Each oxygen atom picks up a carbon atom and they fly off together as carbon monoxide. This is a chemical reaction. The atoms have not changed. They have simply rearranged their partners. The carbon and oxygen atoms were attached to their own kind. Now they are attached to each other. In the process, energy is released. A large amount of kinetic energy is generated. This is the heat of burning. Feynman says nature does not care what we call it. Whether we call it physical or chemical, she just keeps on doing it. Is sawaal mein atoms ka rearrangement hi chemical reaction hai. Yaad rakhiye, atoms kabhi destroy nahi hote, sirf partners badalte hain.

tagline: The jiggling that proved atoms exist!
question_text: How does the Brownian motion of a tiny particle suspended in water provide evidence for the existence of atoms?
option_a: (A) The particle moves in a straight line at constant speed
option_b: (B) The particle is bombarded unevenly by water molecules, causing random jiggling
option_c: (C) The particle dissolves in the water
option_d: (D) The particle emits light due to atomic vibrations
correct_answer: Correct Answer: (B) The particle is bombarded unevenly by water molecules, causing random jiggling
equations_json: ["\\text{Small particle in water}", "\\text{Unequal molecular bombardments}", "\\text{Random motion}", "\\langle R^2 \\rangle = 6kTt/\\mu"]
audio_script: If atoms are always in motion, how can we see them? We cannot see them directly. But Feynman says we can see their effects. Put a tiny particle in water. It is much bigger than the atoms. The water molecules bombard it from all sides. Sometimes more hit one side than the other. The particle jiggles around. This is Brownian motion. It was first seen by Robert Brown in 1827. But it was Einstein who explained it in 1905. He showed that the mean square distance the particle moves is proportional to time. This provided direct evidence for atoms. Feynman says everything is made of atoms. And the Brownian motion proves it. Is sawaal mein atoms ki reality ka sabse pyaara proof hai. Yaad rakhiye, chhota particle bada particle ko dhakka deta hai.

question_text: Ice has a hexagonal crystal structure. What does this mean for the arrangement of water molecules in ice?
option_b: (B) The molecules form a six-sided pattern that repeats in three dimensions
option_c: (C) The molecules form a cubic lattice like salt
option_d: (D) The molecules move freely like in liquid water
correct_answer: Correct Answer: (B) The molecules form a six-sided pattern that repeats in three dimensions
equations_json: ["\\text{Hexagonal symmetry in ice}", "\\text{Six-fold rotational symmetry}", "\\text{Snowflakes show hexagonal pattern}"]
audio_script: In ice, every oxygen atom has a definite place. The water molecules are arranged in a pattern that repeats over and over. This pattern has hexagonal symmetry. If you turn it by sixty degrees, it looks the same. That is why snowflakes have six sides. Feynman says this is one of the beautiful things about crystals. The arrangement of atoms has a symmetry. And that symmetry shows up in the shape of the crystal. Ice also has holes in its structure. When ice melts, these holes can be filled by molecules. That is why ice shrinks when it melts. Most substances expand when they melt. But water is special. Feynman says this is why ice floats. Is sawaal mein crystal ki symmetry aur ice ki anomaly dono hain. Yaad rakhiye, hexagonal symmetry ki wajah se snowflake ke chhe konne hote hain.
